readerTitle: Churchill's war on long memos: why writing short forces you to think
caseNote: 실제 사례 (1940년 8월 처칠의 'Brevity' 메모) + 가상 적용 (주택 리모델링 견적, 물류창고 보고)
insight: 짧게 쓰는 것은 독자의 시간을 아끼는 예의이기 전에, 쓰는 사람이 무엇이 핵심인지 결정했는지 검증하는 도구다.
misconception: 보고서는 길수록 철저하고 성의 있다. 짧게 쓰면 대충 생각한 것처럼 보인다.

sources.text: Winston Churchill, memorandum 'Brevity', 9 August 1940, War Cabinet papers, The National Archives (UK), CAB 67 series
Churchill Archive Centre, Churchill College, Cambridge: Churchill Papers (copies and discussion of the 'Brevity' memo)
주택 리모델링 견적과 물류창고 사례는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: 메모 날짜(1940년 8월 9일)와 제목 'Brevity'는 널리 인용됩니다. 국립기록원 문서번호(CAB 67/8 계열로 알려짐)는 게시 전 원문으로 확인하세요.

cards.title: Churchill's war on long memos
body: August 1940. Britain had just watched France fall and feared an invasion of its own. The Prime Minister had a war to run.
So Winston Churchill sat down and wrote a memo about... the length of memos. He thought it was worth his time. He was probably right.

image.label: A desk buried under stacks of typed reports in a 1940s office
image.brief: 1940년대 영국 정부 집무실. 책상 위에 타자로 친 보고서 더미가 천장 가까이 쌓여 있고, 그 사이에 얇은 종이 한 장만 깔끔하게 놓여 있음. 실존 인물의 얼굴은 그리지 않고 뒷모습이나 손만. 따뜻한 세피아 톤.

cards.title: You're drowning in paper.
body: You lead a government at war. Every department sends you reports, and most run for pages. Key facts sit buried in the middle. You lose hours hunting for the point.
What do you do?

options.text: Hire more aides to read reports and write you summaries
options.feedback: You get shorter pages, but the writers never learn to find their own point. And each summary adds a new person who might miss what matters.

options.text: Tell everyone how to write: main points first, short paragraphs, detail in an appendix
options.feedback: It costs writers more effort up front. But it fixes the problem at the source and makes every writer decide what their point is.

options.text: Only read reports from your most senior ministers
options.feedback: It saves time today. But you'd cut yourself off from the people closest to the facts, and bad news from below would stop reaching you.

cards.title: A memo called "Brevity".
body: On 9 August 1940, Churchill sent his War Cabinet a short memo. It began plainly: we all have to read a mass of papers, and "nearly all of them are far too long."
He asked for four things:
list: Set out the **main points** in short, crisp paragraphs
Put complex analysis and statistics in an **appendix**
Often, replace a full report with a list of headings, explained in person if needed
Cut woolly phrases that are mere padding
cards.callout: He took his own advice. The memo fits on one page.

cards.title: Brevity is a thinking tool
body: Most people treat short writing as a favour to the reader. Churchill saw a second benefit. He wrote that the discipline of setting out the real points concisely would be "an aid to clearer thinking."
**Brevity as discipline** means this: you can't write the short version until you've decided what matters. A long report lets the writer avoid that choice. A short one forces it.

image.label: A long scroll of text being squeezed into three short lines
image.brief: 긴 두루마리 문서가 깔때기를 통과해 짧은 세 줄로 나오는 인포그래픽. 깔때기 옆에 "What matters?"라는 질문 라벨. 단순한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Padding hides missing decisions.
body: Churchill mocked phrases like "Consideration should be given to the possibility of carrying into effect...". Notice what that sentence avoids: who will do what, and by when.
Rewrite it short, and you're forced to fill the gap. "We should close the night shift in March." Now there's a claim someone can agree with, argue with or act on.
When a short version feels impossible to write, the problem is usually the thinking, not the writing.
cards.softwareNote: The same test works on a product spec or a status update in a team chat. If the first line can't say what's changing and who decides, the team isn't ready to build yet.

cards.title: A renovation quote that gets signed.
body: A home renovation firm sends homeowners a 12-page quote. Materials, labour, permits, all listed line by line. Many clients stall for weeks.
The owner moves three lines to the top: what we recommend, the total price, and the start date. Everything else goes into an appendix.
The detail is still there for anyone who wants it. But the client can now see the decision in ten seconds, and so can the person who wrote the quote.

cards.title: Short is not the same as vague.
body: Cutting words is easy. Cutting the right words is hard. A report that drops a key risk to look tidy is worse than a long one.
That's why Churchill kept the appendix. Detail moves out of the way. It doesn't disappear.
There's another risk when a powerful boss demands brevity. People may trim uncertainty and bad news first. Ask for short reports, and also ask: what are you unsure about?

cards.title: Now it's a warehouse.
body: You manage a distribution warehouse. Late shipments rose this month, mostly because one conveyor kept breaking down. Your operations director wants a report by Friday.
How do you start it?

options.text: Open with the full monthly data: volumes, every shift, every delay
options.feedback: It looks thorough, but the director has to dig for the cause and your fix. The real point may never get read.

options.text: "Late shipments rose because conveyor 3 failed often. I recommend replacing it. Cost and data in the appendix."
options.feedback: Cause, recommendation and where to find the proof, all in two lines. Writing it also forced you to commit to one fix.

options.text: "Delays rose due to various operational factors that may require further review."
options.feedback: It's short, but it's padding. It hides the one cause you know and asks the director to do your thinking.

cards.title: If you can't say it short, you haven't decided yet.
body: Put the main points first, push the detail into an appendix, and cut phrases that say nothing. The reader saves time. You find out whether you know your point.
**Try it today:** take your next report or email. Write its point in one sentence at the top. If you can't, fix the thinking before the writing.
